note: Listening, A1–B2. Every script here is written for this site, in British English with UK settings, and will be voiced with generated TTS once a provider is wired (BACKEND.speech) – nothing is taken from a coursebook CD, which is why the task shapes follow the exams but the texts do not. Speakers map to a voice in `voices` below; a generator renders one clip per turn and joins them, so a dialogue really has two people in it. Places, firms and councils (Westbridge, Kingsford, Swiftline …) are made up; the UK rules mentioned (seven days of self-certification before a fit note, the six-month limit for the Financial Ombudsman Service) were checked as of 2026-10.

texts.title: Radio feature: recycling and bin day
texts.blurb: Which bin for what – and why plastic causes the most mistakes.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: Most of us recycle every week, but here in Westbridge about a quarter of what goes into the blue bin shouldn't be there. We asked the council's recycling team why.

script.speaker: mann
script.text: The biggest mistake is plastic. Many people think every kind of plastic can go in the blue bin. But it's only packaging – bottles, pots, tubs and trays. A broken plastic toy isn't packaging, so it goes in the black bin with the general rubbish.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: What about yoghurt pots? Do you have to wash them?

script.speaker: mann
script.text: No, a quick rinse is enough – there's no need to use lots of hot water. What's more important is that you never put your recycling in plastic bags. Our machines can't open the bags, so the whole bag ends up as rubbish.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: And there's a change to bin day, too.

script.speaker: mann
script.text: Yes. From the first of April, food waste will still be collected every week, but the black bin only every two weeks. And all bins need to be out by seven in the morning. The new calendar is on the council website.

questions.prompt: Which plastic can go in the blue bin?

texts.title: Team meeting: working from home
texts.blurb: Three positions, one compromise. Follow the arguments – and notice who gives way on what.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: We need to agree a new working-from-home policy by the end of the month. At the moment every department does its own thing, and that keeps causing friction.

script.speaker: mann2
script.text: To my mind, there's a lot to be said for leaving it as it is. The teams are very different – customer support has to be reachable, while the developers need peace and quiet. A single rule wouldn't do justice to either of them.

script.speaker: frau2
script.text: I see your point, but it overlooks something. If each department decides, in practice it's the manager who decides. So it all depends on who your boss is – and that's exactly the unfairness people keep complaining about.

script.speaker: mann2
script.text: That's a fair point. I was less concerned with the departments' freedom than with getting the work done.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: Then let me suggest a framework rather than a fixed number. Everyone can work from home up to three days a week, but each team agrees on one shared office day. That way support is covered and the developers get their quiet days.

script.speaker: frau2
script.text: I could live with that. The only thing that matters to me is that the office day is put in writing and not renegotiated every week.

script.speaker: mann2
script.text: Agreed. I'd just add that we review it after six months to see whether it's working.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: Good. So, to sum up: up to three days at home, one fixed office day per team, in writing, and a review in six months.

questions.answer: Every department does its own thing

texts.title: Interview: getting foreign qualifications recognised
texts.blurb: An adviser explains what “comparable” means – and the most common mistake people make in the process.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: Dr Hughes, many people who move to the UK have a qualification from their home country, and yet they end up working below their level. What's going wrong?

script.speaker: mann
script.text: Usually it isn't the qualification, it's the process. If you want to work in a regulated profession – nursing, medicine, teaching – you have to be registered with the professional body first. In most other jobs you can start straight away, and getting your qualification recognised is voluntary.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: And what exactly is being checked?

script.speaker: mann
script.text: Whether your qualification is comparable, not whether it's identical. Nobody expects your course to have been the same as a British one. The question is whether there are major differences that actually matter for the job. Small differences in the syllabus are completely normal.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: What's the most common mistake?

script.speaker: mann
script.text: Starting too late. You often need official translations and documents from your old university, and getting hold of those can take months. People who only start once they've arrived can easily lose half a year.

script.speaker: frau
script.text: And if the result is only partial recognition?

script.speaker: mann
script.text: Then the decision tells you exactly which gaps you need to close – usually through extra training or a test. It isn't a rejection; it's more like a set of directions. Unfortunately, a lot of people read it as a no and give up.

questions.prompt: In which jobs do you have to be registered first?
options: In regulated professions, such as nursing
questions.answer: In regulated professions, such as nursing

questions.prompt: What does “comparable” mean here?
options: Exactly the same as a British course
questions.explain: “Comparable, not identical” – only major differences that matter for the job count.

questions.prompt: Why can starting late cost so much time?
options: Getting documents and translations can take months
Professional bodies only accept applications once a year
You have to pass an English test first
questions.answer: Getting documents and translations can take months

questions.prompt: What is the most common mistake, according to Dr Hughes?
How should you understand partial recognition?

texts.title: Short talk: volunteering in the UK
texts.blurb: A trend, a problem and a proposal. Tell the main point from the examples.

script.speaker: mann
script.text: Millions of people in the UK give their time for free – in sports clubs, charity shops and food banks, or as school governors. Volunteering is still a big part of everyday life here, but it's changing.

script.speaker: mann
script.text: What has changed above all is the form it takes. People used to join a club or a charity and stay for thirty years. Today many prefer to help with a particular project for a few months, and then move on to something else.

script.speaker: mann
script.text: For organisations, that's a real difficulty. If you need a treasurer or a chair, you'll struggle to find anyone, because those are roles for years, not months. So people are no less willing to help – they're just less willing to commit.

script.speaker: mann
script.text: There's a second point that is often overlooked: volunteering isn't evenly spread. People with higher incomes and more education volunteer noticeably more often. That has less to do with attitude than with time – if you have two jobs, you haven't got an evening left for a committee meeting.

script.speaker: mann
script.text: So if we want more people to get involved, appealing to their sense of duty won't achieve much. What helps is lowering the barriers: short formats, clear tasks, and organisations that are happy to work with people who only stay for three months.

questions.prompt: How has volunteering changed?
options: Short projects instead of long-term roles
Far fewer people volunteer at all
Most volunteers are older people now
questions.answer: Short projects instead of long-term roles

questions.prompt: Why is this a problem for organisations?
options: Some roles have to be filled for years
They don't get enough new members
questions.answer: Some roles have to be filled for years

questions.prompt: According to the speaker, people today are …
options: as willing to help, but less willing to commit
less willing to help than they used to be
only willing to help if they are paid
questions.answer: as willing to help, but less willing to commit

questions.prompt: How does the speaker explain why volunteering isn't evenly spread?
options: By how much free time people have
questions.answer: By how much free time people have
questions.explain: He says it directly: “less to do with attitude than with time”.

questions.prompt: What is the conclusion of the talk?
options: Lower the barriers instead of appealing to duty
questions.answer: Lower the barriers instead of appealing to duty
